title: A development indicator table: what HDI and GII show and hide

table.caption: Development indicators (invented data for practice). For GII, lower means less gender inequality.

parts.label: A
parts.prompt: Identify the country in the table with the most gender inequality.
parts.sample: Country T, which has the highest GII (0.62).

parts.label: B
parts.prompt: Describe the relationship between girls' expected years of school and the total fertility rate shown in the table.

rubric.point: Describes an inverse relationship with data: countries where girls expect more years of school have lower fertility.
accept: as girls' schooling rises, fertility falls (P: 17 years, TFR 1.5; T: 7 years, TFR 5.6)
an inverse or negative relationship, with table values

parts.sample: The relationship is inverse: where girls expect more years of school, fertility is lower. Country P has 17 years of school for girls and a total fertility rate of 1.5, while Country T has 7 years and a rate of 5.6.

parts.label: C
parts.prompt: Explain why Country Q's HDI is lower than its GNI per capita would suggest.

rubric.point: Uses the table (Q has more than twice R's income but a similar or lower HDI) and explains why: income is not turning into health and schooling, for example because income is unequally shared or comes from a few exports, and girls get less schooling.
accept: Q earns 30,000 to R's 12,000 but has a similar HDI, because the income is concentrated and not spent on health and education
Q's girls expect only 11 years of school, so the education part of HDI is low

parts.sample: Country Q has a GNI per capita of 30,000 dollars, more than twice Country R's 12,000, yet its HDI (0.78) is almost the same as R's (0.76). This is because the HDI also counts health and schooling, and Q's girls expect only 11 years of school, so its income is not being turned into education and health for most people, which pulls its HDI down.

parts.label: D
parts.prompt: Explain ONE reason the HDI is a better measure of development than GNI per capita alone.

rubric.point: Explains that the HDI adds health (life expectancy) and education (schooling) to income, so it shows whether income becomes better lives.
accept: it adds life expectancy and schooling, so it shows more than money
it shows whether income is turned into health and education

parts.sample: The HDI is better because it adds life expectancy and years of schooling to income, so it shows whether a country turns its income into longer, better-educated lives, which GNI per capita, an average of income, cannot show.

parts.label: E
parts.prompt: Explain ONE thing the Gender Inequality Index shows about a country that the HDI does not.

rubric.point: Explains that the GII shows the gap between women and men (in reproductive health, empowerment such as seats in parliament and schooling, or paid work), which the HDI averages over everyone.
accept: the gap between women and men in paid work
women's share of seats in parliament and secondary schooling
deaths in childbirth and teenage births

parts.sample: The GII shows the gap between women and men, for example in seats in parliament and in paid work, because it compares the two groups, whereas the HDI gives one average for the whole population and so hides how women fare compared with men.

parts.label: F
parts.prompt: Explain ONE limitation of using the national data in the table to describe development within Country S.

rubric.point: Explains that national averages hide differences at a smaller scale: between regions, cities and rural areas, or women and men inside Country S.
accept: one national value hides differences between regions or between cities and the countryside
the data are at the national scale, so they cannot show local or regional patterns

parts.sample: The table gives one national value for Country S, so it hides differences inside the country: a capital city may have far more schooling and income than rural regions, and an average of 4,500 dollars can describe almost nobody's life.

parts.label: G
parts.prompt: Explain the degree to which raising girls' schooling in Country T would change its development indicators.

rubric.point: States a degree, then explains with a mechanism: more schooling for girls lowers fertility and the GII and raises the education part of HDI, but income and health depend on other factors too.
accept: to a large degree: more schooling raises HDI's education part, lowers fertility and narrows the GII
to a moderate degree: schooling helps HDI and GII, but income and health care need other changes

parts.sample: To a moderate degree, because more years of school for girls would raise the education part of T's HDI and lower its GII, and educated women tend to marry later and have fewer children, so the fertility rate of 5.6 would fall over time; but T's very low income (1,800 dollars) and health care also hold its HDI down, and schooling alone would not change those quickly.
